meta.schema: same as step_2_rules/rules.json + relation_to_existing; part_ids/conflict_note omitted (not part of the merge)

rules.name: Text card = key words, not the narrated sentence
rules.when: Any on-screen text, label or card shown while narration plays
rules.action: Show only what the voice can't hold: names, numbers, place names, key terms (a few words). Never print the full sentence being spoken as a separate text card. Long explanation goes in the voice, not in on-screen text.
rules.why: Duplicate on-screen text next to narration plus a picture hurts learning; key terms pulled from the narration help more than verbatim text.
rules.evidence_note: Mayer 2008 redundancy d=0.72 (5/5 tests), modality d=1.02 (17/17); Adesope & Nesbit 2012 meta-analysis (57 studies): key terms extracted from narration beat verbatim text; spoken+written beats spoken-only only for picture-free material. Lab learning studies, mostly students; not vlog retention.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-089 (sharpens 'text = jo bola nahi gaya' with the key-terms evidence). Does NOT apply to the bottom caption track — see S-002.

rules.name: Same-language captions stay on for Hindi/Hinglish videos
rules.when: Every long-form and reel with Hindi/Hinglish narration
rules.action: Keep a full same-language caption track (Devanagari or the script the audience reads), timed to the voice, in the bottom band. Treat it as a separate layer from text cards; don't add a second verbatim text block in the middle of the frame.
rules.why: In India, same-language subtitles on Hindi TV songs were read by viewers and linked to literacy gains; captions strongly help viewers who are not fully fluent in the spoken language.
rules.evidence_note: Kothari & Bandyopadhyay 2014, ITID (n=7,409, 5 Hindi states, 2002-2007): SLS viewers showed greater literacy gains (quasi-experimental, self-selected viewers). Montero Perez 2013 captions for second-language video g=0.99 (via Noetel 2022). Outcome is literacy/comprehension, not YouTube retention. Conflicts on its face with Mayer redundancy; the two are about different layers.
rules.relation_to_existing: SUPPORTS R-115 (captions hamesha) with real evidence for this audience; resolves tension with R-089/S-001.

rules.name: Hindi caption reading speed: up to 22 characters per second
rules.when: Every Hindi/Devanagari caption event
rules.action: Keep each caption at or below 22 characters per second (count spaces and punctuation), max 42 characters per line, max 2 lines, prefer one line. For children's content use 18 cps.
rules.why: This is the industry limit Netflix sets for Hindi; English limits (20 or 17 cps) are stricter than needed for Hindi.
rules.evidence_note: Netflix Hindi Timed Text Style Guide: 42 chars/line, 2 lines max, adult up to 22 cps, children up to 18 cps (SDH 25/20). Netflix counts spaces and punctuation. Industry spec for subtitles, not a study.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-092 (20 cps English -> 22 cps for Hindi) and R-131 (~17 cps is too strict for Hindi). New check kind 'max_cps' needed in engine.

rules.name: Caption event duration 0.83 s to 7 s
rules.when: Every caption event
rules.action: No caption shorter than 5/6 s (20 frames at 24 fps) or longer than 7 s; split longer ones.
rules.why: Too short can't be read; too long goes stale and blocks the frame.
rules.evidence_note: Netflix Timed Text Style Guide General Requirements: minimum 5/6 s per event, maximum 7 s. Platform spec.
rules.relation_to_existing: DUPLICATES part of R-092 / R-131 (adds a machine check for both ends).

rules.name: Don't slow or trim captions below the speech
rules.when: Choosing caption wording and speed
rules.action: Keep captions verbatim and in sync with the voice. Only condense when a line would go above the cps limit (S-003). Don't stretch or simplify captions just to make them 'slow'.
rules.why: Viewers keep up with fast subtitles; slow subtitles cause re-reading and less enjoyment; the best subtitle speed is the speech speed.
rules.evidence_note: Szarkowska & Gerber-Moron 2018, PLOS One (n=74, eye-tracking, 12/16/20 cps): viewers coped with fast subtitles; slow subtitles triggered re-reading and frustration. BBC R&D 2015: best subtitle speed = speech speed; verbatim preferred. Interlingual subtitles, European viewers; not Hindi same-language captions.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-091 (that formula is for text cards; don't apply it to captions) and R-131.

rules.name: Vertical reels: about 25 characters per caption line
rules.when: Captions on 9:16 reels/shorts
rules.action: Keep caption lines to about 25 characters (BBC's equivalent of 37 characters on 16:9) so text stays big on a phone.
rules.why: Same physical text size on a narrow frame fits fewer characters.
rules.evidence_note: BBC Subtitle Guidelines: 37 characters in a 75%-width 16:9 region ~= 25 characters in a 90%-width 9:16 region (stated 'as a guide'). Broadcaster guideline.
rules.relation_to_existing: COMPATIBLE with R-247 (max 3 words) and R-259; gives a character ceiling for Devanagari/Hinglish where word counts vary.

rules.name: Picture on screen while its words are spoken
rules.when: A photo, map highlight, clip or card that illustrates a spoken phrase
rules.action: Show the visual during the phrase that names it, not well before or after. If a photo of 'Dwarkadhish mandir' exists, it should be on screen while that name is spoken.
rules.why: Words and matching pictures presented at the same time are learned far better than when one follows the other.
rules.evidence_note: Mayer 2008 temporal contiguity d=1.31 (8/8); Ginns 2006 g=0.78 (via Noetel 2022). Studies compare simultaneous vs successive whole segments; the 1.0 s tolerance in the check is an editorial threshold (🟠), not from the studies.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-088 (replaces its weak coherence citation with the right principle) and RELATED to R-098, R-462.

rules.name: Map labels sit on the map, next to the place
rules.when: Route maps, location maps, annotated photos
rules.action: Put each label right next to the point or object it names (on the map), not in a side legend or a separate card. Keep the narrated place and its label together.
rules.why: Learners do much better when words are placed near the part of the graphic they describe.
rules.evidence_note: Mayer 2008 spatial contiguity d=1.12 (5/5); Schroeder & Cenkci 2018 g=0.63 (k=58), backed by eye-tracking (via Noetel 2022). Static diagrams/lessons; maps inferred to be similar.
rules.relation_to_existing: NEW (no existing rule on label placement on maps).

rules.name: Signal the one thing being talked about
rules.when: Map or photo with several possible points of interest while narration names one
rules.action: Add a cue on the named point at the moment it is named: highlight, pulse, arrow, or a short move toward it. One cue at a time. Use section title cards to signal structure.
rules.why: Cues that point attention to the relevant part improve learning, more so for viewers new to the topic and with moving (dynamic) cues.
rules.frequency: Each time narration names one of several visible things
rules.evidence_note: Schneider et al. 2018 meta-analysis g=0.43 (k=209); Alpizar et al. 2020 d=0.38, stronger for multimedia, low prior knowledge and dynamic signals (both as reported in Noetel 2022). Mayer 2008 signaling d=0.52 (6/6).
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-126 (gives it measured support for graphics/stills) and RELATED to R-378 (caption word highlight).

rules.name: Cut decorative elements, especially ones that stay on screen
rules.when: Stickers, looping background animations, decorative borders, logo bugs, ornamental text
rules.action: Remove any visual that doesn't carry the story or the place. If something decorative must stay, don't keep it on screen for long; brief is less harmful than persistent.
rules.why: Irrelevant 'seductive' details lower learning, mostly when they stay on screen.
rules.evidence_note: Sundararajan & Adesope 2020: removing seductive details g=0.33 (k=68); persistent on-screen details g=0.43 vs transient g=0.12 (CI crosses zero) (via Noetel 2022). Mayer 2008 coherence d=0.97 (13/14).
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-089 / R-312; REPLACES the attention reason of R-231 (Cutting 2018 found clutter unimportant for moment-to-moment attention).

rules.name: Big breaks only at event boundaries
rules.when: Placing chapter cards, section titles, music stops/changes, long transitions, ad-like pauses
rules.action: Put every big break exactly where the event changes (new goal, new action, new place with a stated purpose). Never place a big break in the middle of an event.
rules.why: Breaks at event boundaries improve recall; breaks inside events hurt memory.
rules.evidence_note: Schwan, Garsoffky & Hesse 2000 (n=40): cuts at breakpoints led to more detailed recall. Boltz (reported in Zacks et al. 2007 review): commercials at boundaries improved recall, at non-boundaries impaired it. Zacks 2010: boundaries track situation changes. Feature-film/everyday-activity clips.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-177 and R-178 (moves the evidence from 'any cut' to 'big breaks'); SUPPORTS R-057 and R-087. New check kind 'must_align'; tolerance is editorial.

rules.name: A new section must change the goal, not just the place
rules.when: Starting a new section / chapter
rules.action: Make the new goal or action clear in narration or a card ('ab hum X ki taraf chalte hain', 'yahan darshan ka samay'). A place change alone is a weak boundary. More changes at once make a stronger boundary; save several-at-once for chapter starts.
rules.why: Viewers mark new events mostly when action/goal changes; space or time jumps alone matter little; the chance of a boundary rises with the number of changes.
rules.evidence_note: Magliano & Zacks 2011: action discontinuities had the biggest effect; space/time 'minor effects'. Zacks 2010: probability of segmenting rose with the number of situation changes. Narrative-film studies.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-055 and R-056 (corrects which change matters most).

rules.name: Many photo changes inside one event are fine
rules.when: Several stills/clips cover the same moment (same place, same goal)
rules.action: You may change pictures often within one event; keep them visually continuous (same place, similar tone). Don't treat every photo change as a 'new event' or a jolt. Save boundary signals (cards, music change) for real event changes (S-011).
rules.why: A cut by itself does not create a new event for the viewer; continuity cuts inside a scene often go unnoticed.
rules.evidence_note: Zacks 2010: 'Cuts in and of themselves did not produce increases in segmentation.' Schwan 2000: segmentation 'largely unaffected by the occurrence of cuts'. Smith & Henderson 2008: 25.1% of within-scene and 32.4% of match-action cuts were missed vs 9.4% between-scene. All live-action film; applying to stills is inference.
rules.relation_to_existing: CORRECTS R-178 (its 'jolt/error' claim is not supported) and R-177's 'invisible cut' reason.

rules.name: Slow the cutting at emotional peaks
rules.when: Emotionally intense beats (darshan, aarti, arrival, a personal moment)
rules.action: Don't stack fast cutting on top of an already intense moment. Hold shots longer and let the content carry the arousal.
rules.why: Fast pace plus arousing content overloads viewers and lowers what they recognise and recall.
rules.frequency: At beats tagged as emotional peaks
rules.evidence_note: Lang, Bolls, Potter & Kawahara 1999, J. Broadcasting & Electronic Media: fast pace + arousing content -> less recognition and cued recall (TV messages, lab). No numeric shot length given; threshold left to profiles.
rules.relation_to_existing: SUPPORTS R-176 (speed ceiling) with peer-reviewed evidence; complements R-175 (shots lengthen at the end of the climax).

rules.name: Film shot length is a reference, not a target, for stills
rules.when: Setting shot-length targets for long-form stills/maps/cards
rules.action: Use about 4 s (modern Hollywood mean) only as a talking point. Calibrate real targets on our own format (e.g. R-394 travel reference) per profile; don't fail a stills video for being above 3-6 s.
rules.why: Hollywood ASL fell from about 10 s to under 4 s, but those shots carry motion, and short modern shots carry the most motion; stills have none.
rules.evidence_note: Cutting et al. 2011: ASL ~10 s (1930s-40s) -> below 4 s after 2000 (160 films); shorter shots have proportionately more motion in modern films. Cutting et al. 2018: ~10 s (1950) -> ~4 s (2010). Cutting 2010: 1/f slope did not correlate with IMDb ratings (r=-.089 n.s.). Number is 🟢; using it for stills is inference.
rules.relation_to_existing: CORRECTS R-135 (~4-5 s -> ~4 s, below 4 s after 2000) and MODIFIES R-173 (should not be a hard check for long-form stills; conflicts with R-394).

rules.name: Move the still toward what the voice names
rules.when: Adding a slow zoom/pan to a still photo or map
rules.action: Make the move purposeful: push or pan toward the detail the narration is naming at that moment, and end on it. Avoid random decorative drift with no link to the words.
rules.why: Motion that matches the narration guides eyes to the named detail and helped story recall; moving scenes coordinate viewers' gaze more than static ones.
rules.evidence_note: No direct adult study of Ken Burns moves was found. Closest: Takacs & Bus 2016 (children n=39): motion matched to narration -> more fixation on named detail, better recall. Smith & Henderson 2010 (VSS conference abstract): gaze clustered more in dynamic than static versions of the same scene (15% vs 20% of screen). Kumar et al. 2026 ISR: more background motion raised view-rate on children's YouTube videos (A/B). Children-only or abstract-level evidence.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-205, R-220, R-329, R-357 (gives a purpose rule; their % numbers stay 🟠).

rules.name: Key subject near centre when a new still or card appears
rules.when: First second after a new photo, map or text card
rules.action: Place the key subject or key words near the screen centre at entry (or start the move from centre toward it). Don't put the only important detail in a far corner at the cut.
rules.why: Right after a new image appears, viewers look at the screen centre for about a second before exploring.
rules.evidence_note: Smith & Henderson 2010 (VSS abstract): scenes began with ~1200 ms of high synchrony as all viewers attended to screen centre. Mital et al. 2011 report a central tendency after cuts.
rules.relation_to_existing: SIMPLIFIES R-232 (eye-trace landing) for stills; R-232 itself should be 🟡.

rules.name: First 30 seconds match the title and thumbnail
rules.when: Opening of every long-form video
rules.action: Make sure what the title/thumbnail promise is seen or heard inside the first 30 s, and review the 'Intro' number in YouTube Analytics after release.
rules.why: YouTube's own retention report defines 'Intro' as % still watching after 30 s and advises matching title/thumbnail and reworking the first 30 s.
rules.evidence_note: YouTube Help 'Measure key moments for audience retention' (official platform guidance). YouTube gives 30 s; it does not state a 5 s rule.
rules.relation_to_existing: DUPLICATES R-001 / R-061 (confirms with the official source; the 5 s value in R-001 stays creator data).

rules.name: Explain in short segments with clear breaks
rules.when: Dense explanation (temple history, legend, route logistics)
rules.action: Break it into short segments, each with one idea, separated by a visible or spoken break, and mirror long ones as YouTube chapters so viewers can jump.
rules.why: Segmented material is learned better than one continuous block; the original effect is for learner-paced segments, which chapters partly give.
rules.frequency: Every explanation longer than one idea
rules.evidence_note: Segmenting: Mayer 2008 d=0.98 (3/3, learner-paced); Rey et al. 2019 g=0.32 retention / 0.36 transfer (via Noetel 2022). Guo et al. 2014: median engagement at most 6 min regardless of video length (edX). YouTube chapters: 00:00 start, >=3 timestamps, >=10 s each.
rules.relation_to_existing: SUPPORTS R-153 and R-087 (duplicate check); adds the learning evidence.

rules.name: Introduce key names before the dense part
rules.when: A section that will use many names (deities, places, people)
rules.action: Before the dense part, introduce each key name once with its picture and a short label, then use it.
rules.why: Knowing the names and look of key parts first makes the later explanation easier to learn.
rules.evidence_note: Mayer 2008 pretraining d=0.85 (5/5). Lab lessons; for devotional/travel this is an inference about names, not mechanisms.
rules.relation_to_existing: NEW.

rules.name: Hindi narration speed: warn outside 115-230 wpm, don't fail at English bands
rules.when: Checking narration speed
rules.action: Use 115-230 wpm as hard outer limits and treat 160-195 (R-163) as a soft English-derived guide only. For Hindi/Hinglish, judge pace by ear and by caption cps (S-003) before cutting words.
rules.why: Viewers rated about 175 wpm as right, about 230 too fast and about 115 too slow; word-length differences make English wpm bands unreliable for Hindi.
rules.evidence_note: BBC R&D 2015 (English news-style clips, hearing and hearing-impaired viewers): ~230 wpm 'too fast', ~115 'too slow', ~175 'about right'. Applying to Hindi is inference; Dwarika measured 200.1 wpm, inside these limits.
rules.relation_to_existing: MODIFIES R-163 (keeps it as a warning band, adds evidence-based outer limits).

rules.name: Captions move away from on-screen text
rules.when: Captions would overlap a text card, map label or title
rules.action: Move captions (e.g. to the top) or time them so they never cover on-screen text; when both can't fit, show the more story-relevant one.
rules.why: Overlapping text can't be read; the platform spec requires avoiding overlap.
rules.evidence_note: Netflix TTSG General Requirements: position subtitles to avoid overlap with on-screen text; if unavoidable, place where easier to read. Netflix Hindi TTSG: give precedence to the most plot-pertinent message. Platform spec.
rules.relation_to_existing: RELATED to R-376 (title zones) and R-095 (safe zones).
